lesson.title: Turn a calculation into a tool

steps.headline: A function packages a calculation under a name, and return hands its answer back.

lead.text: def gives a calculation a name. Its parameters receive arguments when you call it. return sends a value back to the caller. print only writes text on the screen.
A function that never reaches return hands back None.
The parameter x receives the argument you pass in. return sends the result of the line back to where the function was called.

reveal.text: You predicted what comes back to the caller. Return gives the caller the value; a function that only prints would hand back None.

cases.label: Case A

steps.headline: With def pay(hours, wage=10): return hours * wage, what do pay(3) and pay(wage=12, hours=2) give?

workedSteps.text: pay(3) gives hours the value 3. No wage is passed, so the default 10 is used.
pay(wage=12, hours=2) names each parameter, so the order does not matter.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

steps.headline: With def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate, what does cost(rate=6, units=5) return?

workedSteps.text: Keywords name the parameters. So units is 5 and rate is 6.
Multiply the two. What does cost return?

lead.text: A parameter is another name for the object you passed in. A method like append changes that object, so the caller sees it. Assigning a new list to the parameter only renames it inside the function.

reveal.text: The function reached the caller's list through its parameter, so the appends were visible outside. Rebinding the parameter would not have been.

lead.text: import makes a module's names available. import math as m gives it the shorter name m. math.ceil rounds up to the next whole number. Importing does not install a missing package.

reveal.text: The alias m is only a local name for the module. m.ceil is math.ceil, and the package had to be available before the import could work.

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import math as m
result = m.sqrt(81)

lesson.orientation: Define functions, pass arguments, return values and import installed libraries.
lesson.reviewLabel: Turn a calculation into a tool
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A card on the till says: cost = units × rate, and the rate is 5 unless the card says otherwise. The card says nothing else.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a function call and tell what return gives back that print does not.

recap.keyIdea: A function takes arguments through its parameters and hands a value back with return; print only displays, and import makes a module's names available.

blocks.text: You priced the card at £15, called triple(7) for 21, and found cost(rate=6, units=5) gives 30. You also saw m.ceil(4.2) round up to 5.

recap.nextHook: Next: catch expected failures, and read files without leaving them open.

questions.prompt: def triple(x): return x * 3. What does triple(7) return?
hints: Put the argument in place of the parameter.
The parameter x receives the argument 7.
Apply the multiplication by 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The argument 7 is multiplied by 3 and returned as 21.

questions.onCorrect: 21. The argument 7 went into x, and return sent x * 3 back.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the argument. The function returns the argument multiplied by 3.

hints: Match each keyword to its parameter name.
units is 5 and rate is 6.
Multiply the two values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Keyword arguments assign units = 5 and rate = 6, so the product is 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. The keywords set units to 5 and rate to 6, replacing the default rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the default rate 4. Here rate=6 replaces it.
That adds the values. The function multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A function prints 12 but has no return statement. What does the call return?
hints: Think about the value handed to the caller, not the text shown on screen.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Printing and returning are separate. A function that reaches the end without return produces None.

questions.onCorrect: None. Printing shows text, while a function with no return statement hands back None.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 was displayed, not handed back. The call itself returns None.
return is a keyword, not a value. Without it, the call gives None.

questions.prompt: After import math as m, what is m.ceil(4.2)?
hints: m is the alias for the math module.
ceil rounds up, not to the nearest.
Which whole number is just above 4.2?
questions.onCorrect: 5. m is the math module under a short name, and ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds down. ceil rounds up.

questions.prompt: def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate. What does cost(8) return?
hints: Use the default for the missing argument.
No rate was passed.
Multiply the units by the default rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The omitted rate uses the default 4: 8 × 4 = 32.

questions.onCorrect: 32. The omitted rate takes its default of 4, so the call computes 8 × 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the default rate. The function multiplies.
That ignores the rate. The default 4 still multiplies.

hints: Find the non-negative square root.
A square root reverses squaring.
Which whole number multiplied by itself gives 144?
questions.onCorrect: 12. The square root reverses squaring, and 12 × 12 is 144.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves 144. A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to give it.

hints: Which line gives a value back to the caller?
print only writes the text on screen.
Work out what return sends back for x = 3.
questions.prompt: def f(x): print(x); return x + 1. After y = f(3), what number does y hold?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The function prints 3 and returns 3 + 1 = 4, so y holds 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. print showed 3 on screen, but only return decides what y holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was printed. y holds what return sent back.

hints: Which rate applies when the card says nothing else?
The cost multiplies units by the rate.
Work out 3 × 5.
questions.prompt: What does 3 units cost, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 units at the default rate 5 cost 15.

questions.onCorrect: £15. The default rate of 5 applies unless you say otherwise. A default argument works exactly this way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds units and rate. The card says units × rate.
That is the number of units. Multiply by the rate.

hints: How does Python know which value is the wage?
questions.prompt: Why does the order of the two arguments not matter here?

choices.label: Each keyword names the parameter it fills

acceptedIdeas: Each keyword names the parameter it fills
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keyword arguments name their parameters, so Python can match them in any order.

questions.onCorrect: Each keyword names the parameter it fills, so position does not matter.

misconceptions.feedback: The product comes out the same either way, but the reason is the keywords.
Python uses the names to choose which parameter each value fills.

hints: Does the parameter refer to the caller's list or to a copy?
append changes the object it is called on.
Start with the original items and add two.
questions.prompt: def grow(items): items.append(7); items.append(8). With values = [1, 2, 3, 4] and the call grow(values), what is len(values)?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The function appends two items to the caller's list, so it now has six.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The parameter and values refer to one list, so both appends are visible to the caller.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. The parameter names the same list, so the appends show in values.
